title: Whisper speech-to-text hallucinations
organization: Cornell University; University of Washington; New York University; University of Virginia

cells.title: Source
body: Allison Koenecke, Anna Seo Gyeong Choi, Katelyn X. Mei, Hilke Schellmann, and Mona Sloane published "Careless Whisper: Speech-to-Text Hallucination Harms" for FAccT 2024.
The arXiv version was submitted on February 12, 2024.

cells.title: Observed behavior
body: The paper evaluated OpenAI's Whisper speech-to-text service and found that some transcriptions contained entire phrases or sentences that were not present in the audio.
The authors reported that hallucinations occurred more often for audio with longer non-vocal durations, including speech from people with aphasia.

cells.source: Careless Whisper, arXiv abstract and Cornell Chronicle summary
cells.label: Study scale and rates

cells.source: Cornell Chronicle summary of Careless Whisper
cells.output: In one example, Whisper correctly transcribed a simple sentence, then added five additional sentences containing words such as terror, knife, and killed, none of which were in the original audio.
The authors reported hallucinated stock phrases such as thanks-for-watching-style language in transcription outputs where the underlying audio did not contain those words.

cells.title: Provenance
body: Primary source: FAccT 2024 paper and arXiv record.
The file also uses Cornell's university summary to identify a concrete example without reproducing a long table.

cells.title: Notes
body: The paper reported an OpenAI Whisper behavior observed as of 2023.
This case records transcription hallucination, not text-chat hallucination.
